title: pjm capacity market woes spur activity bilateral power deals  reeii 2026 08 26
text:
August 26 - Despite soaring demand from data centers and a large volume of power generation under development, PJM's July capacity auction for 2028/29 fell 6.8 GW short of its target as prices hit maximum levels. This was the second consecutive auction to miss the minimum reserve margin.
PJM is the U.S.' largest power network spanning Eastern and Central areas and its capacity pricing model for power ​generation was designed two decades ago, in a time of more predictable load growth and project development. Investors in dispatchable fossil fuel power plants were willing to accept annual auction revenues as sufficient return and in subsequent ‌years PJM adapted the auction model to accommodate rising renewable energy capacity.
CHART: PJM RPM reserve margins, clearing prices
Once again, the operator is reviewing its market design and incentives, in response to unprecedented demand from large loads and delays to power generation projects due to supply chain and permitting issues. Soaring demand is outpacing new generation and PJM estimates new large loads will increase by 70 GW by 2038.
There is no shortage of proposed new power generation, but developers say capacity payment prices and timelines are insufficient and projects are taking longer ​to develop amid supply chain, permitting, and workforce challenges. Over 50 GW of power projects have grid connection agreements and are ready to be developed while 220 GW are under evaluation in PJM's grid connection queue.
To accelerate new power generation, PJM ​has introduced a one-time Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) auction and a parallel process to facilitate bilateral power deals between generators and large loads which could support new power capacity.
Some projects are already moving forward, ⁠buoyed by cap and floor prices implemented by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in 2025 in response to spiking PJM auction prices and bilateral contracts. Since then, developers in the region have announced over 43 GW of projects, mostly in data center hubs in Ohio ​and West Virginia, according to PJM Power Providers Group.
Some developers are already "unwinding some of the challenges and seeing where the investment opportunities exist,” said Todd Snitchler, CEO of the Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA).
“Capital is flowing even as we're sorting out what's going on with PJM's longer-term ​market reform effort."
Short-term reform
PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) auction will offer higher prices and longer contracts than previous auctions. Alongside this, PJM will offer a matchmaking process for new power projects and large loads to secure bilateral deals.
Bilateral contracting was highly preferred among members and PJM “supports bilateral activity to bring new load onto the system,” the grid operator said in July.

The bilateral matchmaking process could support development of new power projects, as capacity market revenue alone is not enough to justify new investments, Ari Pribadi, Global co-head of Investment Banking at Marathon Capital, told Reuters Events.
The matchmaking process ​allows power developers to build on optimum sites away from the data center sites, Pribadi noted.
“This is the right policy. Rather than trying to jam a power plant and a data center in a co-located area, this scheme will enable power plants and data centers ​to be located where each one of them makes sense to be built,” he said.
CHART: Forecast power demand growth by US region
The bilateral matchmaking process opened in June and will continue for six to nine months with ‌the first matches ⁠expected to be disclosed to participants in August.
The scheme allows parties to tailor contract structure, including tenure and pricing, to their needs.
"Certainly, bilateral contracting for new capacity is the preferred way for everyone for this new capacity to enter the market," Glen Thomas, president of the PJM Power Providers Group association and president of regulatory consulting firm GT Power Group.
"If the new large loads can step up [and] sign these bilateral contracts to build the new capacity, it will get developed."
Higher price caps
PJM's RBP auction has a price cap of $555/MW-day for new generation, far higher than the $325/MW-day price cap in the latest capacity auction in July.
Pending approval by FERC, the auction is scheduled to start in late September and close in October with results released by December. Loads that sign bilateral contracts will be excluded from the estimated procurement target ​in the auction. Projects in the bilateral matching process that do ​not secure agreements may bid into the auction.
PJM's July auction ⁠procured 138.3 GW for 2028/29, but only 317 MW came from new generation and 208 MW from upgrades that cleared at the maximum price.

Earthrise Energy CEO Jeff Hunter said the company is “comfortable” with the prices offered in PJM's annual capacity auctions for its existing natural gas-fired plants in the region, but said the caps are not ​sufficient to attract new dispatchable resources at scale.
“All of our assets are contracted, so we're not too concerned about it, but as we look forward, if I were going to do a ​new development somewhere, thermal [natural gas-fired] or ⁠solar or batteries, I would probably look for other markets first,” Hunter told Reuters Events.
The higher price cap for the RBP should allow capacity procurement of new natural gas and battery projects, assuming they sign a 15-year contract, according to Julia Hoos, head of USA East (PJM, NYISO, ISO-NE, SERC) at Aurora Energy Research.
“The hope is that projects that are eligible to participate in the RBP are fairly advanced because they need to construct in the next couple of years and they should have a reasonable handle on what their costs will be,” Hoos noted.
However, Curt Morgan, CEO of ⁠independent power producer ​Alphagen, expects only plant upgrades and late-stage development projects that acquired equipment at lower cost to clear in the auction. Most new projects will need higher prices ​than the cap, he said.
AlphaGen plans to participate in the RBP with around 400 MW of upgrades to existing assets, Morgan said. AlphaGen seeks to develop another 2.3 GW of uprates and expansions with natural gas units at its existing PJM sites in Maryland, New Jersey and Ohio. The company is pursuing long-term bilateral arrangements with ​large loads, mainly data centers, to support capital investment.
“Using our expansion projects as an example, which are in [Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative] states in PJM, and assuming contract terms through 2042, we are seeing a need for capacity payments in the $1,285 to $1,665/MW-day for new-build projects,” he said.
